q-65173.name: Question 1
q-65173.problem: Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$
q-65173.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-71399.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$
q-71399.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(0,0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,k \\  & =({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }j+({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,0) & =({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,i+({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,j+({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $2\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

q-130718.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$
q-130718.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-131126.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=5.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,2).$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)k \\  & =(2xy+{z}^{2})\,i+({x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+2zx)\,k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(2(1)(-1)+(2)^{2})\text{ }i+((1)^{2}+2(-1)(2))\text{ }j+((-1)^{2}+2(2)(1))\text{ }k \\  & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,-1,2)$ and passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,∇f(1,-1,2)=⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface x2y+y2z+z2x=5 at the point (1,−1,2).

a
 ⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨4,5,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
 ⟨−2,5,−3⟩+t⟨1,−1,2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 ⟨2,3,−5⟩+t⟨1,−1,2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
 ⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨2,−3,5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
 ⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨−2,5,−3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's set f(x,y,z)=x2y+y2z+z2x. Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=5.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (1,−1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−1,2).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (1,−1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2y+y2z+z2x)i+∂∂y(x2y+y2z+z2x)j+∂∂z(x2y+y2z+z2x)k=(2xy+z2)i+(x2+2yz)j+(y2+2zx)k∇f(1,−1,2)=(2(1)(−1)+(2)2) i+((1)2+2(−1)(2)) j+((−1)2+2(2)(1)) k=2i−3j+5k=⟨2,−3,5⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(1,−1,2) and passes through the point (1,−1,2) can be written as

r=⟨1,−1,2⟩+t∇f(1,−1,2)=⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨2,−3,5⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).
